notes: Each pair is one term (label) matched to one description. 'short' targets 8-12 words, 'long' targets about 14-22 words, so the page can test either length. 'type' is 'definition' or 'scenario'. Terms come from the glossary (terms.json); 'term' keeps the glossary spelling and 'label' is the cleaned display name.

pairs.label: Confirmation Bias
pairs.short: Dev only reads articles that agree with what he already believes.
pairs.long: Dev only clicks on articles that agree with what he already believes and scrolls past anything that challenges him.

pairs.label: Hindsight Bias
pairs.short: After the game ends, Mia insists she knew who would win.
pairs.long: After the game ends, Mia insists she knew all along who would win, even though she never said so beforehand.

pairs.label: Overconfidence
pairs.short: Believing your judgments are more accurate than they truly are.
pairs.long: The tendency to be more sure of your beliefs and judgments than the evidence justifies, like predicting an easy A.

pairs.label: Case Study
pairs.short: Close examination of one person or group, hoping to reveal universal principles.
pairs.long: Researchers closely examine one person or small group in great depth, hoping the details reveal principles that apply to everyone.

pairs.label: Convenience Sample
pairs.short: Surveying only the students who happened to be near the vending machine.
pairs.long: A researcher surveys only the students who happened to be standing near the vending machine because they were easy to reach.

pairs.label: Experimenter Bias
pairs.short: Researcher's expectations unintentionally influence how a study turns out.
pairs.long: A researcher's hopes about the results subtly influence participants or how data are recorded, pushing the outcome toward what they expected.

pairs.label: Hypothesis
pairs.short: A specific, testable prediction about how variables are related.
pairs.long: A specific, testable prediction about how two or more variables are related, usually written as an if-then statement.

pairs.label: Meta-Analysis
pairs.short: Statistically combines results from many studies to find an overall trend.
pairs.long: A statistical technique that pools the results of many independent studies on one topic to reveal an overall conclusion.

pairs.label: Naturalistic Observation
pairs.short: Priya quietly records how toddlers play at the park without interfering.
pairs.long: Priya sits on a bench and quietly records how toddlers behave at the park without trying to change anything.

pairs.label: Operational Definition
pairs.short: Researchers count how many times a child hits to measure 'aggression.'
pairs.long: To measure 'aggression' precisely, researchers spell out exactly what counts: the number of times a child hits another child during recess.

pairs.label: Peer Review
pairs.short: Experts critique a scientist's paper before a journal will publish it.
pairs.long: Before a journal publishes a scientist's paper, other experts in the field evaluate whether the research is accurate and credible.

pairs.label: Social Desirability Bias
pairs.short: Sam says he exercises daily on a survey because it sounds good.
pairs.long: On a survey, Sam claims he exercises every day, though he doesn't, because he wants to look good to others.

pairs.label: Confounding Variable
pairs.short: Tutored students scored higher, but they also happened to sleep more.
pairs.long: In a tutoring study, tutored students scored higher, but they also happened to sleep more, so sleep could explain the result.

pairs.label: Control Group
pairs.short: Participants who do not receive the treatment, serving as a comparison.
pairs.long: The participants in an experiment who do not get the treatment, giving researchers a baseline to compare the treated participants against.

pairs.label: Dependent Variable
pairs.short: The quiz score researchers record after testing different note-taking styles.
pairs.long: Researchers test three note-taking styles and then record each student's quiz score, the outcome that may change.

pairs.label: Double-Blind Procedure
pairs.short: Neither participants nor researchers know who received the real treatment.
pairs.long: Neither the participants nor the staff running the study know who received the real treatment and who got an inactive pill.

pairs.label: Falsifiability
pairs.short: A scientific claim must be capable of being proven wrong.
pairs.long: For a claim to count as scientific, there must be some possible evidence that could show it is false.

pairs.label: Illusory Correlation
pairs.short: Jo believes her lucky socks cause wins, though the two are unrelated.
pairs.long: Jo is convinced her lucky socks cause her team to win, even though the two are completely unrelated.

pairs.label: Independent Variable
pairs.short: The type of music researchers assign each group to hear while studying.
pairs.long: Researchers have some students study with music and others in silence, deliberately changing this factor to see its effect.

pairs.label: Placebo Effect
pairs.short: Lena's headache improves after taking a sugar pill she thought was medicine.
pairs.long: Lena's headache improves after she takes a sugar pill, simply because she expects the pill to be real medicine.

pairs.label: Random Assignment
pairs.short: Researchers draw names from a hat to decide each student's condition.
pairs.long: Researchers draw names from a hat to decide by chance which condition each student receives, minimizing preexisting differences.

pairs.label: Confederates
pairs.short: Actors pose as participants but secretly follow the researcher's script.
pairs.long: In a conformity study, several actors pretend to be ordinary participants but secretly follow the researcher's script.

pairs.label: Debriefing
pairs.short: After a study, researchers explain its true purpose and any deception.
pairs.long: After participants finish, researchers explain the true purpose of the study, reveal any deception used, and answer questions.

pairs.label: Informed Consent
pairs.short: Before the study, Ben reads about risks and chooses to participate.
pairs.long: Before the study begins, Ben is told its purpose, procedures, and risks, and then voluntarily agrees to take part.

pairs.label: Institutional Review Board
pairs.short: Committee that approves studies by checking they protect participants' safety.
pairs.long: A committee that examines proposed studies in advance to make sure they are ethical and protect participants' rights and well-being.

pairs.label: Likert Scales
pairs.short: Survey items ask you to choose from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree.'
pairs.long: Survey items ask you to rate how much you agree, choosing anywhere from 'strongly disagree' to 'strongly agree.'

pairs.label: Qualitative Research
pairs.short: Researchers interview students and analyze the feelings they describe in words.
pairs.long: Researchers interview students about test anxiety and analyze the feelings and experiences they describe in their own words instead of numbers.

pairs.label: Bimodal Distribution
pairs.short: A graph of exam scores shows two separate peaks.
pairs.long: A graph of exam scores shows two separate peaks, one cluster of low scores and another of high scores.

pairs.label: Effect Size
pairs.short: Measures how big or meaningful a difference or relationship actually is.
pairs.long: Shows the strength or practical importance of a result, going beyond whether a difference exists to how big it is.

pairs.label: Median
pairs.short: The middle score when all scores are lined up in order.
pairs.long: The score in the exact middle of an ordered list, with half the scores above it and half below.

pairs.label: Negative Skew
pairs.short: Most students scored high, with a few very low scores.
pairs.long: On an easy quiz most students scored high, while a few very low scores stretch a long tail to the left.

pairs.label: Normal Curve
pairs.short: Symmetrical bell-shaped graph where most scores fall near the average.
pairs.long: A symmetrical, bell-shaped graph in which most scores cluster near the mean and fewer scores appear at the extremes.

pairs.label: Percentile Rank
pairs.short: Zoe scored better than 85 percent of the people who tested.
pairs.long: Zoe learns she scored higher than 85 percent of all test takers, a number that tells her position among them.

pairs.label: Standard Deviation
pairs.short: Shows how spread out scores are from the mean.
pairs.long: A low value means most scores sit close to the average, while a high value means scores are widely scattered.

pairs.label: Statistical Significance
pairs.short: A result unlikely to have happened by chance alone (p-value).
pairs.long: A statement that an obtained result is very unlikely to have occurred by chance alone, usually shown by a small p-value.

pairs.label: Behavioral Perspective
pairs.short: Maya studies hard because past A's earned her rewards.
pairs.long: A psychologist explains Maya's study habits by pointing to the rewards and consequences in her environment that shaped her actions.

pairs.label: Biological Perspective
pairs.short: A psychologist links Ravi's mood swings to hormones and brain chemistry.
pairs.long: A psychologist explains Ravi's mood swings by examining his genes, hormones, and brain chemistry rather than his upbringing.

pairs.label: Cognitive Perspective
pairs.short: A psychologist studies how students think, remember, and solve problems.
pairs.long: A psychologist studies how people mentally process information, such as how they think, remember, and solve problems.

pairs.label: Humanistic Perspective
pairs.short: A therapist emphasizes each client's potential for personal growth and fulfillment.
pairs.long: A therapist focuses on each healthy client's free will and potential for personal growth rather than on past conflicts.

pairs.label: Psychodynamic Perspective
pairs.short: A therapist explores how Leo's hidden childhood conflicts drive his actions.
pairs.long: A therapist explores how Leo's unconscious drives and unresolved childhood conflicts shape the way he acts and feels today.

sets.title: Unit 1 Quilt: Biological Bases of Behavior

pairs.label: Epigenetics
pairs.short: How experiences can switch genes on or off without altering DNA.
pairs.long: How environmental factors such as stress or diet change gene expression without changing the DNA sequence itself.

pairs.label: Monozygotic Twins
pairs.short: Two siblings formed from one egg that split, sharing nearly all genes.
pairs.long: Two siblings formed when a single fertilized egg split in two, so they share nearly all of their genetic material.

pairs.label: Natural Selection
pairs.short: Faster antelope survive predators, reproduce, and pass speed to offspring.
pairs.long: Antelope with a speed advantage survive predators, reproduce more, and pass that helpful trait to the next generation.

pairs.label: Central Nervous System
pairs.short: The brain and spinal cord, which coordinate the body's responses.
pairs.long: The division made up of the brain and spinal cord, which processes information and directs the body's responses.

pairs.label: Somatic Nervous System
pairs.short: Chen deliberately lifts his arm to raise his hand in class.
pairs.long: Chen deliberately lifts his arm to raise his hand, using the division that controls voluntary skeletal muscle movement.

pairs.label: Sympathetic Nervous System
pairs.short: Walking into a dark alley, Lila's heart races and her pupils dilate.
pairs.long: Walking alone into a dark alley, Lila's heart races and her pupils dilate as her body prepares for fight or flight.

pairs.label: Acetylcholine
pairs.short: Neurotransmitter that triggers muscle contractions and helps form memories.
pairs.long: A neurotransmitter that lets neurons communicate with muscles and also plays an important role in learning and memory.

pairs.label: Action Potential
pairs.short: A neuron's brief electrical impulse racing down its axon.
pairs.long: After enough stimulation, a neuron fires a brief electrical impulse that travels down its axon to the next cell.

pairs.label: Agonists
pairs.short: Chemicals that bind to receptors and mimic a neurotransmitter's effect.
pairs.long: Drug molecules that bind to receptors and activate them, copying or increasing the effects of a natural neurotransmitter.

pairs.label: Dopamine
pairs.short: Andre feels a rush of reward after winning the game.
pairs.long: Andre feels a surge of motivation and pleasure after winning the game, thanks to this reward-related neurotransmitter.

pairs.label: Endorphins
pairs.short: A runner feels pain relief and euphoria from natural opiate-like chemicals.
pairs.long: After a long run, Eliza feels less pain and a wave of euphoria from the body's natural, morphine-like chemicals.

pairs.label: GABA
pairs.short: Raj's anti-anxiety medication boosts the brain's main calming, inhibitory messenger.
pairs.long: Raj takes anti-anxiety medicine that boosts the brain's main inhibitory neurotransmitter, helping neural activity quiet down so he can relax.

pairs.label: Leptin
pairs.short: Grace stops eating when her fat cells signal she's full.
pairs.long: Grace stops eating because a hormone released by her fat cells tells her brain that she has enough stored energy.

pairs.label: Melatonin
pairs.short: Yuki gets sleepy at night as this hormone rises.
pairs.long: As evening darkness falls, Yuki's brain releases more of this hormone, which makes her sleepy and helps regulate her sleep.

pairs.label: Myelin Sheath
pairs.short: Fatty insulation around axons that speeds up neural signals.
pairs.long: A fatty insulating layer wrapped around many axons that lets electrical impulses travel faster down the neuron.

pairs.label: Reflex Arc
pairs.short: Isa's hand jerks off a hot pan before she feels pain.
pairs.long: Isa touches a hot pan and her hand jerks away automatically before her brain even registers the pain.

pairs.label: Reuptake
pairs.short: Sending neurons reabsorb leftover neurotransmitters from the synapse to clear it.
pairs.long: After a signal is sent, the sending neuron reabsorbs leftover neurotransmitter from the synapse, clearing it and regulating signal strength.

pairs.label: Tolerance
pairs.short: Pablo needs more coffee than before to feel the same alertness.
pairs.long: Pablo now needs more coffee than he used to in order to feel the same alertness, because his body adapted.

pairs.label: Amygdala
pairs.short: Almond-shaped limbic structure involved in fear, aggression, and emotional memories.
pairs.long: A small, almond-shaped structure in the limbic system involved in processing emotions, especially fear and aggression, and forming emotional memories.

pairs.label: Aphasia
pairs.short: After a stroke, Luca struggles to speak or understand words.
pairs.long: After damage to language areas of his brain, Luca struggles to speak, understand, read, or write words.

pairs.label: Cerebellum
pairs.short: While learning to ride a bike, Katie's balance and coordination improve.
pairs.long: Katie's balance and muscle coordination improve as she learns to ride a bike, guided by this rear brain structure.

pairs.label: Corpus Callosum
pairs.short: Thick band of fibers connecting the brain's left and right hemispheres.
pairs.long: A thick band of neural fibers that lets the left and right halves of the brain communicate with each other.

pairs.label: EEG
pairs.short: Electrodes on Rachel's scalp record her brain waves while she sleeps.
pairs.long: A doctor places electrodes on Rachel's scalp to record the electrical waves sweeping across her brain while she sleeps.

pairs.label: Hippocampus
pairs.short: Isabella forms new memories of her trip using this seahorse-shaped structure.
pairs.long: Isabella forms new memories of her vacation and learns her way around a new city using this seahorse-shaped structure.

pairs.label: Hypothalamus
pairs.short: Small brain structure regulating hunger, thirst, temperature, and hormone release.
pairs.long: A small brain structure that helps regulate hunger, thirst, body temperature, and hormone release by controlling the endocrine system.

pairs.label: Medulla
pairs.short: Brainstem part controlling vital involuntary functions like breathing and heart rate.
pairs.long: A part of the brainstem that controls vital involuntary functions such as breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure.

pairs.label: Plasticity
pairs.short: The brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections.
pairs.long: The brain's ability to change and reorganize itself by forming new neural connections in response to learning, experience, or injury.

pairs.label: Occipital Lobes
pairs.short: Cortex at the back of the brain that processes visual information.
pairs.long: The part of the cerebral cortex at the back of the brain that is primarily responsible for processing visual information.

pairs.label: Circadian Rhythm
pairs.short: The body's internal 24-hour clock regulating the sleep-wake cycle.
pairs.long: The body's internal biological clock that regulates the sleep-wake cycle and other physiological processes on a roughly 24-hour schedule.

pairs.label: Hypnagogic Sensations
pairs.short: Ravi, drifting off to sleep, suddenly feels like he is falling.
pairs.long: As Ravi drifts off to sleep, he suddenly feels like he is falling or floating, a vivid dreamlike experience.

pairs.label: Narcolepsy
pairs.short: Victor suddenly falls asleep in the middle of a conversation.
pairs.long: Victor has uncontrollable sleep attacks during the day and can drop into sleep without warning, even mid-conversation.

pairs.label: REM Rebound
pairs.short: After staying up late, Amira spends extra time in dream sleep.
pairs.long: After being deprived of dream sleep one night, Amira spends much more time in it the next night.

pairs.label: Sleep Apnea
pairs.short: Jorge's breathing repeatedly stops during the night, waking him many times.
pairs.long: Jorge's breathing repeatedly stops and starts at night, causing him to gasp and wake momentarily many times.

pairs.label: Somnambulism
pairs.short: Sophia walks to the kitchen at night with no memory later.
pairs.long: Sophia gets up in the middle of the night and walks to the kitchen while still asleep, remembering nothing.

pairs.label: Blind Spot
pairs.short: Place where the optic nerve exits the eye, containing no receptor cells.
pairs.long: The place where the optic nerve leaves the eye has no receptor cells, so light landing there goes undetected.

pairs.label: Cochlea
pairs.short: Snail-shaped, fluid-filled inner ear structure that converts vibrations into neural signals.
pairs.long: A fluid-filled, snail-shaped structure in the inner ear that converts sound vibrations into neural signals the brain can interpret.

pairs.label: Gate Control Theory
pairs.short: Rubbing a stubbed toe makes the pain feel a little better.
pairs.long: Rubbing a stubbed toe helps because other sensory input can block pain signals passing through the spinal cord to the brain.

pairs.label: Rods
pairs.short: In dim light, Ben sees using retinal cells that can't detect color.
pairs.long: In a dim room, Ben sees using photoreceptors in his retina that are very sensitive to light but cannot detect color.

pairs.label: Sensory Adaptation
pairs.short: Tia stops noticing the strong perfume in the room after ten minutes.
pairs.long: Tia walks into a room with strong perfume, but after ten minutes she barely notices it because her senses adjusted.

pairs.label: Weber’s Law
pairs.short: One pound is noticeable in an empty backpack, not a heavy one.
pairs.long: A one-pound change is obvious in an empty backpack but unnoticeable in a heavy one, because detecting changes depends on proportion.

pairs.label: Change Blindness
pairs.short: Jess misses that her friend got a haircut until told.
pairs.long: Jess doesn't notice her friend's dramatic new haircut until someone points it out, because her attention was elsewhere.

pairs.label: Cocktail Party Effect
pairs.short: In a noisy cafeteria, Omar instantly hears someone say his name.
pairs.long: In a loud cafeteria, Omar focuses on one conversation but still instantly notices when someone across the room says his name.

pairs.label: Figure and Ground
pairs.short: Viewers see a vase in the picture, then notice two faces.
pairs.long: Looking at a famous image, you first see a vase, then your focus shifts and you notice two faces.

pairs.label: Interposition
pairs.short: Your friend's head partly blocks the whiteboard, so she seems closer.
pairs.long: One object partly blocks your view of another, so your brain judges the blocking object to be closer to you.

pairs.label: Phi Phenomenon
pairs.short: Blinking neon arrows at a drive-through look like they are moving.
pairs.long: Neon lights at a drive-through blink on and off one after another, creating the illusion of an arrow moving.

pairs.label: Retinal Disparity
pairs.short: Brain compares slightly different images from each eye to judge depth.
pairs.long: A binocular depth cue in which the brain uses the slight difference between the images seen by each eye.

pairs.label: Top-Down Processing
pairs.short: Using context, Lee easily reads a text full of typos.
pairs.long: Lee easily reads a message full of typos because her expectations and prior knowledge fill in the missing letters.

pairs.label: Algorithms
pairs.short: Step-by-step procedures that guarantee a solution when followed correctly.
pairs.long: Logical, step-by-step procedures that guarantee a solution to a problem if followed correctly, though they can be slow.

pairs.label: Availability Heuristic
pairs.short: After a plane-crash news story, Ana fears flying more than driving.
pairs.long: After seeing vivid news coverage of a plane crash, Ana judges flying to be more dangerous than driving.

pairs.label: Functional Fixedness
pairs.short: Jon can't think to use a coin as a screwdriver.
pairs.long: Jon searches for a screwdriver and never thinks to use a coin, because he sees coins only as money.

pairs.label: Gambler’s Fallacy
pairs.short: After five tails in a row, Leo bets heads is 'due.'
pairs.long: After a coin lands tails five times in a row, Leo is sure heads must be 'due' next.

pairs.label: Prototypes
pairs.short: The most typical example of a category, used to classify new things.
pairs.long: The best or most typical example of a concept, which helps people quickly recognize and classify new objects or ideas.

pairs.label: Sunk-Cost Fallacy
pairs.short: Rob finishes a terrible movie because he already paid for tickets.
pairs.long: Rob sits through a terrible movie he hates because he already paid for the ticket, even though leaving would be better.

pairs.label: Echoic Memory
pairs.short: Nia can still 'hear' her teacher's last sentence for a few seconds.
pairs.long: Even after her teacher stops talking, Nia can still 'hear' the last sentence in her mind for a few seconds.

pairs.label: Episodic Memory
pairs.short: Ivy vividly recalls her tenth birthday party: the cake, friends, and place.
pairs.long: Ivy consciously recalls her tenth birthday party, including when and where it happened, who came, and the cake.

pairs.label: Iconic Memory
pairs.short: A camera flash goes off, and Kai still sees it briefly.
pairs.long: After a camera flash goes off, Kai still holds a fleeting visual image for a fraction of a second.

pairs.label: Long-term Potentiation
pairs.short: Repeated activation strengthens synaptic connections, a neural basis for learning.
pairs.long: A lasting increase in the strength of synapses after repeated firing, believed to be a biological basis for learning.

pairs.label: Phonological Loop
pairs.short: Cam silently repeats a phone number to hold it in mind.
pairs.long: Cam silently repeats a phone number over and over, using the verbal rehearsal system to hold it until he can dial.

pairs.label: Semantic Memory
pairs.short: Ted knows Paris is France's capital, without recalling when he learned it.
pairs.long: Ted knows that Paris is the capital of France, a general fact he has no personal recollection of learning.

pairs.label: Procedural Memory
pairs.short: Lena rides a bike without thinking, her muscles just remember how.
pairs.long: Years after learning, Lena rides a bike automatically without consciously recalling the steps, because her muscles remember how.

pairs.label: Chunking
pairs.short: Remembering FBICIANBA as three familiar acronyms instead of nine letters.
pairs.long: Eli remembers the nine letters FBICIANBA by grouping them into three familiar acronyms instead of memorizing each letter separately.

pairs.label: Massed Practice
pairs.short: Cramming all studying into one long session, which weakens long-term retention.
pairs.long: A learning strategy of studying in a single long session, often called cramming, which usually leads to weaker long-term retention.

pairs.label: Method of Loci
pairs.short: Priya mentally places vocabulary words around rooms of her house to remember.
pairs.long: To remember her vocabulary list, Priya mentally walks through her house and drops each word at a familiar spot.

pairs.label: Primacy Effect
pairs.short: Better memory for items at the beginning of a list.
pairs.long: The tendency to remember items at the start of a list best, because they receive more attention and rehearsal.

pairs.label: Spacing Effect
pairs.short: Information is remembered better when study sessions are spread out over time.
pairs.long: The tendency for information to be remembered better when study sessions are spread out over time instead of crammed into one.

pairs.label: Anterograde Amnesia
pairs.short: After a head injury, Joel can't form new memories but remembers childhood.
pairs.long: After a head injury, Joel cannot form new long-term memories, yet his memories from before the accident remain intact.

pairs.label: Elaborative Rehearsal
pairs.short: Hana connects new vocabulary to things she already knows to remember it.
pairs.long: Hana thinks about the meaning of each new vocabulary word and links it to knowledge she already has, improving retention.

pairs.label: Infantile Amnesia
pairs.short: Adults like Gus cannot remember anything from before age three.
pairs.long: Gus cannot recall learning to walk or eating baby food, because brain structures for memory weren't developed before age three.

pairs.label: Context Dependent Memory
pairs.short: Back in her old classroom, Tess suddenly remembers the forgotten answer.
pairs.long: Back in the classroom where she first learned the material, Tess suddenly recalls the answer she couldn't remember elsewhere.

pairs.label: Metacognition
pairs.short: Awareness of your own thinking, including monitoring and regulating how you learn.
pairs.long: Awareness and understanding of your own thought processes, including the ability to monitor, evaluate, and regulate your learning strategies.

pairs.label: Recognition
pairs.short: Identifying previously learned information when it appears again, like multiple-choice answers.
pairs.long: A memory process of identifying previously learned information when it is presented again, often with the help of cues.

pairs.label: Encoding Failure
pairs.short: Information was never processed into storage, so it can't be recalled.
pairs.long: Information was never processed into long-term storage, so it was never properly stored and cannot be retrieved later.

pairs.label: Misinformation Effect
pairs.short: Witnesses asked about a car 'smashing' into another recall faster speeds.
pairs.long: Witnesses asked how fast cars 'smashed' into each other remember higher speeds, because the wording distorted their memory of the event.

pairs.label: Proactive Interference
pairs.short: Ira keeps writing last year's date; old memories block the new year.
pairs.long: Every January, Ira keeps writing last year's date on his papers because older memories block his recall of the new year.

pairs.label: Tip-of-the-Tongue Phenomenon
pairs.short: Lou knows the actor's name but can't quite retrieve it.
pairs.long: Lou is certain he knows an actor's name and feels it is about to come, but he cannot retrieve it.

pairs.label: Flynn Effect
pairs.short: Average IQ scores have steadily risen from generation to generation.
pairs.long: The observed rise in average IQ test scores across generations, meaning your grandparents would score lower on today's norms.

pairs.label: Growth Mindset
pairs.short: After a low grade, Dara believes more effort will improve her intelligence.
pairs.long: After a low grade, Dara believes her abilities can be developed through effort and persistence, so she keeps practicing.

pairs.label: Reliability
pairs.short: A test gives Ana nearly identical scores each time she takes it.
pairs.long: A test gives Ana nearly identical scores each time she takes it, showing it produces stable, repeatable results.

pairs.label: Stereotype Threat
pairs.short: Reminded of a negative belief about her group, Mei's test score drops.
pairs.long: Mei is reminded that her group is expected to do poorly on math, and the anxiety lowers her score.

pairs.label: Validity
pairs.short: A psychology final made entirely of calculus problems measures the wrong thing.
pairs.long: A psychology final made entirely of calculus problems fails to measure what it is supposed to measure.

pairs.label: Cross-Sectional Studies
pairs.short: Compares people of different ages at one point in time.
pairs.long: Research that compares groups of individuals of different ages at a single point in time to examine developmental differences.

pairs.label: Longitudinal Studies
pairs.short: Researchers follow the same 100 children and retest them for twenty years.
pairs.long: Researchers follow the same 100 children for twenty years, retesting them regularly to see how they change.

pairs.label: Imprinting
pairs.short: A newly hatched duckling follows the first moving thing it sees.
pairs.long: A newly hatched duckling forms a strong attachment to and follows the first moving object it sees, often its mother.

pairs.label: Rooting Reflex
pairs.short: Stroking a newborn's cheek makes her turn and search for food.
pairs.long: When someone strokes a newborn's cheek, she automatically turns her head and opens her mouth, searching for a nipple.

pairs.label: Teratogens
pairs.short: Harmful substances that can cause birth defects during prenatal development.
pairs.long: Harmful substances or agents, such as alcohol, certain drugs, or infections, that can damage a developing baby before birth.

pairs.label: Visual Cliff
pairs.short: Infants hesitate to crawl across a glass table that appears to drop.
pairs.long: In a lab, babies hesitate to crawl over a glass surface that creates the illusion of a drop-off, showing depth perception.

pairs.label: Maturation
pairs.short: Babies crawl before they walk, regardless of how much practice they get.
pairs.long: Babies crawl before they walk, following a biologically driven sequence of development that unfolds largely regardless of practice or experience.

pairs.label: Animism
pairs.short: Believing inanimate objects have thoughts, feelings, or intentions.
pairs.long: A belief common in early childhood that inanimate objects have thoughts, feelings, or intentions, like thinking a toy is sad.

pairs.label: Assimilation
pairs.short: Toddler Mina calls a horse 'doggie,' fitting it into her dog category.
pairs.long: Toddler Mina sees a horse and calls it 'doggie,' fitting the new animal into her existing dog category.

pairs.label: Conservation
pairs.short: Knowing that quantity stays the same even when appearance or arrangement changes.
pairs.long: The understanding that properties like volume, mass, or number stay the same even when an object's appearance or arrangement changes.

pairs.label: Egocentrism
pairs.short: Sam gives Dad his favorite toy, assuming Dad must love it too.
pairs.long: Sam gives his dad his own favorite toy for his birthday, assuming Dad sees things exactly as Sam does.

pairs.label: Object Permanence
pairs.short: Understanding that things keep existing even when they can't be seen.
pairs.long: The understanding that things continue to exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or directly sensed.

pairs.label: Scaffolding
pairs.short: Temporary guidance from a teacher or peer, slowly removed as skills grow.
pairs.long: Temporary support from a teacher or peer that helps a learner finish a task, gradually removed as skills grow.

pairs.label: Theory of Mind
pairs.short: Four-year-old Zane realizes his friend doesn't know the secret hiding spot.
pairs.long: Zane understands that his friend has her own thoughts and doesn't know where the toy is hidden, even though he does.

pairs.label: Morphemes
pairs.short: The prefix 'un-' in 'unhappy' carries its own meaning.
pairs.long: Prefixes like 'un-' and suffixes like '-ed' are the smallest units of language that carry meaning.

pairs.label: Overgeneralization
pairs.short: A toddler proudly says 'mouses' and 'goed' instead of correct forms.
pairs.long: A toddler applies grammar rules too broadly, saying 'mouses' instead of 'mice' and 'goed' instead of 'went.'

pairs.label: Telegraphic Speech
pairs.short: A two-year-old says 'want cookie' instead of a full sentence.
pairs.long: Around age two, a child uses only essential words, like 'want cookie' instead of 'I want a cookie.'

pairs.label: Authoritative Parenting
pairs.short: High expectations combined with warmth, support, and open communication.
pairs.long: A style that combines high expectations with warmth, support, and open communication, encouraging both responsibility and independence.

pairs.label: Identity Foreclosure
pairs.short: Kira plans to be a lawyer like her mother without exploring alternatives.
pairs.long: Kira commits to becoming a lawyer like her mother without ever exploring other possible careers or values.

pairs.label: Imaginary Audience
pairs.short: Theo is sure everyone in the hallway is staring at his pimple.
pairs.long: Theo is certain that everyone in the hallway is staring at his pimple, when others are actually focused on themselves.

pairs.label: Integrity and Despair
pairs.short: Reflecting on his life, Abe feels either fulfillment or deep regret.
pairs.long: In late adulthood, Abe looks back on his whole life and feels either a peaceful sense of fulfillment or overwhelming regret.

pairs.label: Mesosystem
pairs.short: Interactions between parts of a person's immediate environment, like family and school.
pairs.long: In Bronfenbrenner's theory, the connections between different parts of a person's immediate environment, such as the relationship between family and school.

pairs.label: Parallel Play
pairs.short: Two toddlers sit side by side with toys, ignoring each other.
pairs.long: Two toddlers sit side by side busy with their own toys, close together but ignoring each other completely.

pairs.label: Secure Attachment
pairs.short: Toddler Omar explores the playroom, returning to Mom for comfort.
pairs.long: Toddler Omar confidently explores the playroom, uses his mother as a safe home base, and is easily comforted when upset.

pairs.label: Trust and Mistrust
pairs.short: Erikson's first stage: consistent caregiving teaches infants the world is reliable.
pairs.long: Erikson's first psychosocial stage, in which consistent, responsive caregiving teaches infants that the world is safe and reliable.

pairs.label: Acquisition
pairs.short: Milo's cat learns the can opener means food and starts running.
pairs.long: After the can opener sounds before every meal, Milo's cat learns it predicts food and starts running to the kitchen.

pairs.label: Habituation
pairs.short: After a week, Lila no longer notices the ticking classroom clock.
pairs.long: After a week in the same classroom, Lila stops responding to the ticking clock because it is constant and repeated.

pairs.label: Spontaneous Recovery
pairs.short: Weeks after the bell stopped meaning food, the dog suddenly drools again.
pairs.long: Weeks after the bell stopped predicting food and the drooling faded, the dog suddenly drools at the bell again.

pairs.label: Stimulus Discrimination
pairs.short: Max's dog runs to the door only for his car's engine.
pairs.long: Max's dog runs to the door only when she hears his car's engine, ignoring the sounds of other cars.

pairs.label: Taste Aversion
pairs.short: After one bout of illness, Tom refuses to eat sushi again.
pairs.long: After getting sick once following a sushi dinner, Tom avoids sushi for years, even though one meal made him ill.

pairs.label: Unconditioned Stimulus
pairs.short: A puff of air to the eye automatically makes Rae blink.
pairs.long: A puff of air hits Rae's eye and she blinks automatically, without any prior learning needed for the response.

pairs.label: Fixed Ratio
pairs.short: Reward given after a set number of responses.
pairs.long: A schedule that delivers a reward after a set number of responses, producing fast responding with a brief pause afterward.

pairs.label: Learned Helplessness
pairs.short: After failing three quizzes, Noor stops studying, convinced nothing will help.
pairs.long: After failing three quizzes no matter how hard she studied, Noor feels powerless and stops trying altogether.

pairs.label: Negative Reinforcement
pairs.short: Dev takes aspirin and keeps doing it because the headache goes away.
pairs.long: Dev takes aspirin and the headache goes away, so he becomes more likely to take aspirin again next time.

pairs.label: Positive Punishment
pairs.short: Mia comes home late and her parents add extra chores.
pairs.long: Mia breaks curfew, so her parents add extra chores, making her less likely to come home late again.

pairs.label: Shaping
pairs.short: Rewarding successive approximations until the full desired behavior is learned.
pairs.long: A learning process in which each successive approximation of a desired behavior is rewarded until the full behavior is learned.

pairs.label: Variable Interval
pairs.short: Cam checks his phone repeatedly for a text that arrives unpredictably.
pairs.long: Cam keeps checking his phone at a steady pace because a new message might arrive after an unpredictable amount of time.

pairs.label: Cognitive Maps
pairs.short: Mental layout of a physical space that helps you navigate.
pairs.long: A mental representation of the layout of an environment that helps an organism navigate and understand where places are.

pairs.label: Insight Learning
pairs.short: Suddenly, Ray realizes how to solve the puzzle: an 'aha' moment.
pairs.long: After staring at the puzzle without progress, Ray suddenly realizes the solution without any trial and error: an 'aha' moment.

pairs.label: Vicarious Conditioning
pairs.short: Jen watches a classmate get punished for texting and hides her phone.
pairs.long: Jen watches a classmate get detention for texting in class and then keeps her own phone out of sight.

sets.title: Unit 4 Quilt: Social Psychology and Personality

pairs.label: Fundamental Attribution Error
pairs.short: Sam assumes his late friend is lazy, ignoring the traffic accident.
pairs.long: Sam assumes a classmate who arrived late is lazy, overlooking the fact that a traffic accident blocked her route.

pairs.label: Internal Locus of Control
pairs.short: Priya believes her grades come from her own choices and effort.
pairs.long: Priya believes her grades are mainly caused by her own actions, choices, and effort rather than luck or teachers.

pairs.label: Mere Exposure Effect
pairs.short: A song Tara disliked grows on her after hearing it daily.
pairs.long: Tara disliked a new song at first, but after hearing it on the radio all week she loves it.

pairs.label: Relative Deprivation
pairs.short: Leo loved his phone until his friend arrived with a nicer one.
pairs.long: Leo felt thrilled with his upgraded phone until a friend arrived with a newer model, and suddenly felt worse off.

pairs.label: Self-Fulfilling Prophecy
pairs.short: Convinced she'll fail, Ana skips studying and then does fail.
pairs.long: Ana is convinced she will fail, so she stops studying, and her lack of preparation causes the failure she expected.

pairs.label: Self-Serving Bias
pairs.short: Eli takes credit for an A but blames others for a D.
pairs.long: Eli takes full credit for an A, but blames the teacher and unfair questions for a D.

pairs.label: Cognitive Dissonance
pairs.short: Dan knows smoking harms health, yet smokes and feels uncomfortable about it.
pairs.long: Dan knows smoking harms his health, yet he keeps smoking, feeling an uncomfortable tension between his beliefs and his actions.

pairs.label: Ethnocentrism
pairs.short: Believing your own culture is superior and judging others by its standards.
pairs.long: The belief that one's own culture or group is superior to others, leading to judging other cultures by one's own standards.

pairs.label: Just-World Phenomenon
pairs.short: Believing people get what they deserve, so victims must have earned it.
pairs.long: The belief that people get what they deserve, assuming good things happen to good people and bad things to bad people.

pairs.label: Stereotype
pairs.short: Oversimplified belief that all members of a group share the same traits.
pairs.long: A generalized belief about a group of people that assumes all members share the same characteristics, oversimplifying reality.

pairs.label: Altruism
pairs.short: Helping others out of genuine concern, expecting no personal reward.
pairs.long: Helping behavior motivated by a genuine desire to benefit another person without expecting any personal gain or reward.

pairs.label: Bystander Effect
pairs.short: No one helps a fallen student in the crowded hallway.
pairs.long: A student falls in a crowded hallway, and no one helps because everyone assumes someone else will step in.

pairs.label: Conformity
pairs.short: Everyone at school starts wearing the same sneakers, so Ben buys them.
pairs.long: Everyone at school starts wearing the same sneakers and slang, so Ben changes his own style to match the group.

pairs.label: Deindividuation
pairs.short: Lost in a roaring crowd, Ty yells things he'd never say alone.
pairs.long: Anonymous in a roaring stadium crowd, Ty loses self-awareness and yells things he would never say when he is alone.

pairs.label: Door-in-the-Face Technique
pairs.short: Ava asks for a $500 jacket, then happily accepts $20.
pairs.long: Ava first asks her parents for a $500 jacket, and after they say no, she asks for just $20 instead.

pairs.label: Foot-in-the-Door Technique
pairs.short: Cal asks for help with one math problem, then the whole packet.
pairs.long: Cal asks a friend to help with one math problem, and once she agrees, he asks her to do the whole packet.

pairs.label: Groupthink
pairs.short: Desire for harmony makes group members suppress dissent and decide badly.
pairs.long: A phenomenon in which the desire for group harmony leads members to suppress dissenting opinions and make flawed decisions.

pairs.label: Halo Effect
pairs.short: One positive impression of a person makes you assume other good traits.
pairs.long: A bias in which one positive impression of someone shapes judgments of their other traits, like assuming attractive people are kind.

pairs.label: Social Loafing
pairs.short: In a group project, Max puts in less effort than usual.
pairs.long: In a group project where individual contributions aren't tracked, Max puts in much less effort than he would alone.

pairs.label: Superordinate Goals
pairs.short: Objectives rival groups can only reach by cooperating, which reduces conflict.
pairs.long: Shared objectives that require different or rival groups to work together to achieve them, often reducing conflict between those groups.

pairs.label: Displacement
pairs.short: Scolded by his boss, Ken snaps at his little sister.
pairs.long: After being scolded by his boss, Ken holds in his anger and then snaps at his innocent little sister at home.

pairs.label: Id
pairs.short: Primitive, unconscious part of personality that demands immediate gratification of urges.
pairs.long: The primitive, unconscious part of personality that operates on the pleasure principle, seeking immediate gratification of basic drives and desires.

pairs.label: Projection
pairs.short: Mara dislikes her coworker but insists the coworker dislikes her.
pairs.long: Mara secretly dislikes her coworker, but she insists that her coworker is the one who dislikes her.

pairs.label: Rationalization
pairs.short: After cheating, Joe explains that everyone does it so it's fine.
pairs.long: After cheating on a quiz, Joe builds a reasonable-sounding explanation that everyone does it, so it isn't really wrong.

pairs.label: Reaction Formation
pairs.short: Nora secretly likes Jake but acts cold and mean toward him.
pairs.long: Nora has a secret crush on Jake, so she hides her true feelings by acting cold and mean toward him.

pairs.label: Sublimation
pairs.short: Redirecting unacceptable impulses into socially acceptable, productive activities.
pairs.long: A defense mechanism in which unacceptable impulses are channeled into socially acceptable or productive activities, like turning aggression into athletics.

pairs.label: Superego
pairs.short: Lena feels guilty after keeping extra change, hearing an inner voice.
pairs.long: Lena feels guilty after keeping extra change from a cashier, as her internalized sense of right and wrong objects.

pairs.label: Unconditional Positive Regard
pairs.short: A therapist accepts and values her client without judgment, whatever he does.
pairs.long: According to Rogers, a therapist accepts and values her client without judgment or conditions, regardless of his behavior or feelings.

pairs.label: Conscientiousness
pairs.short: Ivy makes a color-coded schedule and meets every deadline early.
pairs.long: Ivy creates a color-coded schedule for her group project, sets deadlines, and reliably finishes everything before they arrive.

pairs.label: Neuroticism
pairs.short: Wes overthinks every text and always expects the worst outcome.
pairs.long: Wes overthinks every casual text for hours, feels anxious and moody, and always expects the worst-case scenario.

pairs.label: Reciprocal Determinism
pairs.short: Thoughts, behavior, and environment all continuously influence one another.
pairs.long: Bandura's idea that a person's thoughts, behavior, and environment constantly interact, and each of these factors also shapes the others.

pairs.label: Self-Efficacy
pairs.short: Ria is confident she can ace her upcoming driver's test.
pairs.long: Ria believes strongly in her own ability to succeed at this specific task, so she is confident she'll ace her driver's test.

pairs.label: Approach-Avoidance
pairs.short: Kai wants to attend the party but dreads seeing his ex.
pairs.long: Kai really wants to attend the weekend party but dreads that his ex will be there, leaving him with mixed feelings.

pairs.label: Boredom Susceptibility
pairs.short: Intolerance for repetitive, monotonous experiences and a craving for novelty.
pairs.long: A component of sensation seeking marked by an intolerance for repetitive or monotonous experiences and a strong desire for novelty and change.

pairs.label: Homeostasis
pairs.short: The body's tendency to maintain a stable internal environment, such as temperature.
pairs.long: The body's tendency to maintain a stable internal environment by regulating conditions such as temperature, hunger, and hydration.

pairs.label: Incentive Theory
pairs.short: Mark studies extra hours because his parents promised him the car.
pairs.long: Mark puts in extra hours of studying because his parents promised him the car if he earns an A.

pairs.label: Intrinsic Motivation
pairs.short: Lila paints for hours purely because she enjoys it.
pairs.long: Lila paints for hours with no prize or grade involved, simply because the activity itself is personally rewarding and enjoyable.

pairs.label: Yerkes-Dodson Law
pairs.short: Moderate nerves sharpen Jo's test performance, but panic makes her freeze.
pairs.long: Moderate pre-test nerves sharpen Jo's focus and performance, but intense panic overwhelms her and makes her perform worse.

pairs.label: Display Rules
pairs.short: Rae smiles and thanks her aunt for an ugly sweater.
pairs.long: Rae forces a big smile and thanks her aunt for an ugly sweater, because her culture expects polite emotions.

pairs.label: Facial-Feedback Hypothesis
pairs.short: Forcing a smile during a bad mood actually lifts Tom's mood.
pairs.long: Tom is in a bad mood, but forcing himself to smile makes him feel a little happier because expressions influence emotions.

sets.title: Unit 5 Quilt: Mental and Physical Health

pairs.label: Eustress
pairs.short: Positive stress that boosts motivation, performance, or well-being.
pairs.long: A positive form of stress that enhances motivation, performance, or well-being, like the excited energy before a big game.

pairs.label: Exhaustion Stage
pairs.short: After months of relentless pressure, Maya's depleted body gets sick.
pairs.long: After months of relentless pressure, Maya's resources run out, leaving her depleted, unable to cope, and often sick.

pairs.label: Fight Flight Freeze Response
pairs.short: Spotting a bear, Cole's heart pounds as his body prepares to react.
pairs.long: Spotting a bear, Cole's heart pounds as his body automatically readies him to confront the danger, escape, or stay still.

pairs.label: Problem-Focused Coping
pairs.short: Overwhelmed by homework, Ari makes a schedule to tackle the actual workload.
pairs.long: Overwhelmed by homework, Ari attacks the source of her stress by making a schedule and breaking assignments into steps.

pairs.label: Tend and Befriend Theory
pairs.short: Under stress, Gwen seeks her peers' support and comforts her cousin.
pairs.long: Under stress, Gwen copes by seeking support from her peers and protecting and nurturing her little cousin.

pairs.label: Gratitude
pairs.short: Positive emotion from recognizing and appreciating kindness or support received from others.
pairs.long: A positive emotional response that comes from recognizing and appreciating the benefits, kindness, or support you have received from others.

pairs.label: Posttraumatic Growth
pairs.short: After surviving a serious illness, Dee feels stronger and values life more.
pairs.long: After struggling through a life-threatening illness, Dee reports newfound inner strength and a deeper appreciation for life.

pairs.label: Resilience
pairs.short: After losing her job, Rosa adapts quickly and keeps functioning.
pairs.long: After losing her job, Rosa adapts to the setback, recovers quickly, and keeps functioning well despite the stress.

pairs.label: Subjective Well-Being
pairs.short: A person's self-reported evaluation of their own happiness and life satisfaction.
pairs.long: A person's self-reported evaluation of their happiness and life satisfaction, including the balance of positive and negative emotions.

pairs.label: Diathesis-Stress Model
pairs.short: An inherited vulnerability only becomes a disorder after overwhelming life pressures.
pairs.long: Mental disorders result when a biological or psychological predisposition is triggered by overwhelming life pressures.

pairs.label: Dysfunction
pairs.short: Thoughts, emotions, or behaviors that interfere with daily functioning.
pairs.long: A criterion for psychological disorders: thoughts, emotions, or behaviors that interfere with a person's ability to handle daily life effectively.

pairs.label: Eclectic Approach
pairs.short: Treatment that combines techniques from multiple therapies based on the individual's needs.
pairs.long: A flexible style of treatment that combines techniques and principles from multiple perspectives or therapies, depending on each person's needs.

pairs.label: Stigma
pairs.short: Employers avoid hiring Cam after learning he was treated for depression.
pairs.long: After learning Cam was treated for depression, employers avoid hiring him because of a negative label attached to mental disorders.

pairs.label: Agoraphobia
pairs.short: Fear of being trapped keeps Ida from leaving home for crowded places.
pairs.long: Ida fears situations where escape might be difficult, so she avoids crowded and open places and rarely leaves home.

pairs.label: Ataque de Nervios
pairs.short: Culture-bound syndrome in Latin American cultures: shouting, trembling after family crisis.
pairs.long: A culture-bound syndrome common in Latin American cultures, with episodes of shouting, crying, and trembling after a stressful family event.

pairs.label: Catatonic Stupor
pairs.short: Hal sits motionless and unresponsive, though his eyes are open.
pairs.long: Hal sits completely motionless and unresponsive, appearing awake with his eyes open, but does not react to anything around him.

pairs.label: Compulsions
pairs.short: Uma feels driven to wash her hands exactly twenty times.
pairs.long: Uma feels driven to wash her hands exactly twenty times, a ritual that briefly eases the anxiety from her obsessive thoughts.

pairs.label: Delusions
pairs.short: Strongly held false beliefs that persist despite clear evidence to the contrary.
pairs.long: Strongly held false beliefs that persist despite clear evidence otherwise, commonly associated with psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia.

pairs.label: Dissociative Amnesia
pairs.short: After a traumatic event, Cora cannot recall important personal information.
pairs.long: After a traumatic event, Cora cannot recall key personal information, a memory loss inconsistent with ordinary forgetting or injury.

pairs.label: Flashbacks
pairs.short: A veteran suddenly feels as though he is reliving combat.
pairs.long: Triggered by a loud noise, a veteran has a vivid, intrusive experience of reliving a traumatic combat event.

pairs.label: Flat Affect
pairs.short: Ned shows almost no emotion in his face, voice, or gestures.
pairs.long: Ned shows little or no outward emotion through his facial expressions, tone of voice, or gestures, a negative symptom.

pairs.label: Generalized Anxiety Disorder
pairs.short: Fay feels continually tense and worried about everything for months.
pairs.long: Fay is continually tense and apprehensive, worrying about grades, health, and the future for months with no specific trigger.

pairs.label: Hallucinations
pairs.short: False sensory experiences, like hearing voices that aren't actually there.
pairs.long: A positive symptom of schizophrenia involving false sensory experiences, such as hearing voices or seeing things that are not actually present.

pairs.label: Hypervigilance
pairs.short: Since the accident, Gus constantly scans every room for danger.
pairs.long: Since his accident, Gus sits facing the door and constantly scans every room for threats, always on high alert.

pairs.label: Mania
pairs.short: Abnormally elevated mood and energy, with impulsivity and little need for sleep.
pairs.long: A state of abnormally elevated mood, energy, and activity that can include impulsivity, decreased need for sleep, and impaired judgment.

pairs.label: Panic Attack
pairs.short: With no danger present, Jax's heart pounds and he can't breathe.
pairs.long: With nothing dangerous happening, Jax is overwhelmed by sudden intense fear, a pounding heart, and shortness of breath that peak within minutes.

pairs.label: Taijin Kyofusho
pairs.short: A man in Japan fears his body odor will offend others.
pairs.long: A man in Japan is intensely afraid his appearance or body odor will offend or embarrass the people around him.

pairs.label: Word Salad
pairs.short: Lee's speech is a jumble of terms that make no sense together.
pairs.long: Lee's speech is strung together incoherently, such as 'purple elephant tree yesterday pizza,' making communication unintelligible.

pairs.label: Active Listening
pairs.short: A therapist carefully reflects and clarifies a client's feelings to show empathy.
pairs.long: A humanistic therapist carefully reflects and clarifies the client's thoughts and feelings so the client feels understood and accepted.

pairs.label: Biofeedback
pairs.short: Using electronic monitoring to gain voluntary control over processes like heart rate.
pairs.long: A technique that uses electronic monitoring to help people gain voluntary control over processes such as heart rate or muscle tension.

pairs.label: Cognitive Restructuring
pairs.short: A therapist helps Ian replace 'I always fail' with realistic thoughts.
pairs.long: A therapist helps Ian identify and challenge his negative thought 'I always fail,' and replace it with more realistic, adaptive thoughts.

pairs.label: Dream Interpretation
pairs.short: A therapist analyzes symbols in Eve's sleeping visions to uncover unconscious conflicts.
pairs.long: A psychodynamic therapist analyzes the content and symbols of Eve's visions while she sleeps to uncover her unconscious thoughts and conflicts.

pairs.label: Electroconvulsive Therapy
pairs.short: Brief electrical currents trigger a seizure to relieve severe depression.
pairs.long: Under anesthesia, a patient with severe depression receives electrical currents to the brain that trigger a brief seizure.

pairs.label: Free Association
pairs.short: Sol says whatever thoughts and memories come to mind without censoring himself.
pairs.long: In therapy, Sol openly says whatever thoughts, feelings, and memories come to mind without censoring them, letting unconscious conflicts surface.

pairs.label: Lithium
pairs.short: A mood stabilizer that reduces manic episodes in bipolar disorder.
pairs.long: A mood-stabilizing medication, a naturally occurring mineral, commonly used to reduce the severity of manic episodes and help prevent mood swings.

pairs.label: Lobotomy
pairs.short: A historic surgery cut nerves linking the frontal lobes to emotional centers.
pairs.long: Once used to calm violent or uncontrollably emotional patients, this surgery cut nerves connecting the frontal lobes to the brain's emotional centers.

pairs.label: Systematic Desensitization
pairs.short: Ben pairs relaxation with gradual exposure to spiders, starting with photos.
pairs.long: To overcome his spider phobia, Ben pairs relaxation with gradual exposure, from photos up to a real spider.

pairs.label: Tardive Dyskinesia
pairs.short: After years on antipsychotic medication, Pat develops involuntary, repetitive facial movements.
pairs.long: After years of taking antipsychotic medication, Pat develops involuntary, repetitive movements of the face and tongue as a side effect.

pairs.label: Token Economies
pairs.short: Students earn points for good behavior and trade them for privileges.
pairs.long: In a classroom program, students earn a point for each desired behavior and later exchange the points for privileges or treats.

pairs.label: Therapeutic Alliance
pairs.short: The collaborative, trusting relationship between therapist and client that supports treatment.
pairs.long: The collaborative, trusting bond between therapist and client that supports effective treatment and positive outcomes.
